lesson: Run simulation at a fixed step (for example 1/60 s) using an accumulator and render once per frame with leftover time as interpolation. Clamp the frame delta (for example 0.25 s) so a tab switch cannot cause a spiral of catch-up updates.
Remember a jump or attack press for about 100-150 ms and fire it as soon as it becomes legal. This removes the feeling that the game ate an input.
Allow a jump for about 80-120 ms after the player walks off a ledge. Reset the timer while grounded and consume it on jump so players do not double jump.

Apply upward velocity on jump press and, if the button is released while rising, cut vertical velocity (multiply by about 0.4-0.5) or increase gravity. Use higher gravity while falling than rising for a snappy arc.

Move the player by accelerating toward a target velocity and applying friction when there is no input, instead of setting velocity directly. Use faster deceleration than acceleration for tight control, and normalize diagonal input so diagonals are not 41 percent faster.

Move on the X axis, resolve overlaps against solid tiles, then move on Y and resolve again. Resolving one axis at a time prevents sticking on walls and corners and works for both platformers and top-down games.
Fast objects can pass through thin walls in one frame. Cap speed below tile size per step, sub-step movement, or sweep the box along its path. Never test only the end position.

Two axis-aligned boxes overlap when a.x < b.x + b.w and a.x + a.w > b.x and a.y < b.y + b.h and a.y + a.h > b.y. Use circle tests (distance squared against radius sum squared) for round actors to avoid square roots.

Store levels as a 2D array of tile ids with a separate table describing each id (solid, hazard, sprite, friction). Convert world to tile with Math.floor(x / tileSize) and only test collision against tiles near the actor.

Smooth the camera toward the target using exponential smoothing (camera += (target - camera) * (1 - Math.exp(-k * dt))) so it is frame-rate independent. Clamp to map bounds and add a small look-ahead in the facing direction.

Add short, decaying screen shake, hit-stop (freeze for 40-80 ms on impact), squash and stretch, particles and a sound for every important event. Scale intensity with the importance of the event and always offer a way to reduce shake.
Every dangerous attack needs a readable wind-up (color flash, sound, animation, ground marker) before damage. Fairness comes from the player being able to see and react to what will hurt them.

Define the 5-30 second core loop (act, get feedback, earn progress) before adding content. If the loop is not fun with placeholder art, more content will not fix it. Add variety by changing how the loop is challenged, not by repeating it.

Introduce each mechanic in a safe space, then test it with a simple challenge, then combine it with earlier mechanics. Avoid text walls; make the first level an implicit tutorial using level layout and one prompt at a time.

Alternate tension and relief: ramp challenge, then give a breather or reward. Increase difficulty with new combinations rather than only bigger numbers, and give players a small comeback path after failure (checkpoints, short retries).
Make death-to-retry take under two seconds with one key press. Short failure cost makes players willing to take risks and keeps them playing.
Place the best rewards behind visible risk so choice is meaningful. Every option should be best in some situation; if one choice is always best, the others are dead content.
For any currency, list every source and sink and estimate income per minute. If sources outrun sinks, the currency becomes meaningless; add scaling costs, upkeep or choices that spend it.

Use a required-XP curve such as xp_to_next = base * level^1.5 so early levels come fast and later levels slow. Keep power growth and enemy growth on the same curve family so players feel stronger without trivializing content.
A robust formula is damage = max(1, attack * (100 / (100 + defense))). It keeps defense useful at every level, never reaches zero damage and never makes a character invulnerable.

Use a seedable PRNG (mulberry32 or a similar small generator) instead of Math.random for anything that must be reproducible: level generation, loot, replays and bug reports. Keep separate generators for gameplay and cosmetic effects.
Pick from a weighted table by summing weights, drawing r in [0, total) and subtracting weights until r goes below zero. For fairness add pity systems that raise odds after repeated misses.

Generate dungeons by placing non-overlapping rooms, connecting centers with L-shaped corridors in order (or a minimum spanning tree), then adding a few extra loops. Verify every room is reachable with a flood fill before accepting the level.

Fill a grid randomly (about 45 percent walls), then repeat 4-5 times: a tile becomes a wall if five or more of its eight neighbors are walls. Keep only the largest connected region to guarantee a playable cave.

Layer several octaves of Perlin or simplex noise (each with double frequency and half amplitude) for natural terrain, and map elevation thresholds to biomes. Use a second noise field for moisture to vary biomes.

For generated puzzles or levels, build the solution first and then scramble it with legal reverse moves, or run a solver/flood fill to verify solvability. Reject and regenerate instead of shipping an unwinnable level.

A* explores nodes by lowest f = g + h using a priority queue, where h is an admissible heuristic: Manhattan distance for 4-way grids, octile for 8-way, Euclidean for free movement. Cache paths and recompute only when the target moves a tile or the map changes.

When many units go to one goal, run one breadth-first search outward from the goal to build a distance field, then each unit steps to the neighbor with the lowest distance. It is cheaper than running A* per unit and supports tower defense rerouting.

Model enemies as explicit states (idle, patrol, chase, attack, flee) with transitions driven by sensed conditions. Add hysteresis (a larger radius to lose a target than to gain it) and minimum state times to stop flickering.

Use selector nodes (first child that succeeds) and sequence nodes (all children must succeed) with condition and action leaves for layered AI. They scale better than large state machines when behaviors are shared.

Combine simple forces: seek, flee, arrive (slow within a radius), separation (avoid neighbors) and alignment/cohesion for flocking. Sum weighted forces, clamp to a max force and speed, and integrate each frame.
Give enemies a vision cone (distance plus angle) with a line-of-sight check and a short reaction delay, and a memory of the last known position. Delays and memory make AI feel fair and readable.

Reuse bullets, particles and enemies from a pre-allocated pool with an active flag instead of creating and destroying them every frame. This avoids garbage collection stutter in JavaScript and allocation spikes in other engines.
For many moving objects, bucket them in a grid keyed by cell and only test collisions against objects in the same and adjacent cells. This turns an O(n squared) pass into roughly O(n).

Decouple systems with a small event emitter (on, off, emit) so achievements, audio and UI react to gameplay events without gameplay code knowing about them. Unsubscribe when objects are destroyed to avoid leaks.

Compose behavior from small components (position, velocity, sprite, health) and systems that process entities having them, rather than deep inheritance trees. It makes adding new enemy types a data change.
Represent actions as objects with execute and undo. This gives you rebindable input, replays (store the command stream), AI using the same actions as players and undo for puzzle games.

Put enemy stats, items, levels and dialogue in data tables (JSON or resource files) and keep code generic. Designers and generators can then add content without touching logic, and balancing becomes editing numbers.
Keep an explicit game state (title, playing, paused, game over) with enter, update, draw and exit hooks per state. Pausing is just not updating the playing state while still drawing it.
Save plain serializable data (JSON) with a version number and migrate old versions on load. In browsers use localStorage inside try/catch, and validate loaded data before trusting it.
Multiply all movement and timers by delta time in seconds so speed does not depend on frame rate. Express speeds in units per second, not per frame.

Pre-render static layers (tile backgrounds) to an offscreen canvas and draw it once per frame, round draw positions to integers for crisp pixels, batch draws by image, and avoid creating objects or strings in the render loop.

Render at a small internal resolution (for example 320 by 180) and scale the canvas up with CSS image-rendering: pixelated and context.imageSmoothingEnabled = false. Scale by integer multiples to avoid shimmering.
Letterbox the canvas to keep the aspect ratio, and convert pointer coordinates through the canvas bounding rect and scale factor so clicks and touches land on the right world position.

Browsers block audio until a user gesture, so create or resume the AudioContext on the first key press or click. Without asset files, synthesize effects with oscillators and gain envelopes (short attack, exponential decay) and vary pitch slightly per play to avoid repetition.

Make retro effects from an oscillator whose frequency sweeps quickly (jump up, hit down), a noise burst for explosions, and a gain ramp to zero. Cap simultaneous sounds so a burst of events does not distort.

Use pointer events for mouse and touch together, call preventDefault on touch to stop scrolling, track multiple pointers by id and provide on-screen controls at least 44 pixels in size when targeting phones.

Track held keys in a set from keydown and keyup, and separately record pressed-this-frame for single actions. Use event.code (physical key) for movement so layouts do not matter, and clear state on window blur to avoid stuck keys.

Without image assets, build sprites from simple shapes with a limited palette (5-8 colors), strong silhouettes, a dark outline and consistent lighting direction. Give each entity type a distinct shape and color so players identify them instantly.

Keep hazards and pickups visually distinct from the background, use value contrast not only hue (many players are color blind), pair color with shape or icon, and keep the player the most visible element on screen.
Show only what the player needs now (health, ammo, objective), place it at screen edges, animate changes (flash on damage, count up on score) and make text large enough to read at a glance.
A game needs a start screen with controls, a pause menu, a game over screen with the score and a one-key retry. Show controls in the first seconds of play and let any key start.
Offer rebindable or alternate controls, avoid time pressure on essential inputs where possible, provide volume and screen shake toggles and never rely on color alone to convey information.

Design levels around the jump's measured range (max height and distance) with safe margins. Teach a hazard in safety first, then repeat it with variation, then combine it. Place checkpoints before hard sections.

Zelda-style games gate progress with items and knowledge: a hub overworld, dungeons each granting a tool, and obstacles that require that tool. Use locked doors, switches and one-way shortcuts so players loop back to earlier areas.

Build the world as a grid of screen-sized rooms with exits to neighbors, loading one room at a time with its enemies and objects. Transition with a short slide or fade and keep persistent state (opened chests, killed bosses) in a save table keyed by room id.

Track keys, items and switch states as flags. Create a dependency graph (item A opens door B leading to item C) and verify by simulation or graph search that the end is reachable and that no key can be locked behind its own door.
Give attacks anticipation, a brief active hitbox window and recovery. Use hit-stop, knockback and invulnerability frames after damage (about 0.5-1 s with blinking) so the player is not chain-hit.

Structure bosses as phases with clear telegraphed patterns, a vulnerability window after each attack and a new behavior when health crosses thresholds. Reuse the mechanics the player learned earlier in the dungeon.
Show dialogue in a box with typewriter text that can be skipped, store dialogue as data nodes with choices and flags, and let NPC lines change with game state so the world reacts to progress.
Represent items by id plus count in a dictionary, with item definitions in a data table. Stack consumables, cap inventory sensibly and show tooltips so players always know what an item does.
Keep a turn order queue sorted by speed, a clear action menu and visible previews of damage or status. Separate the battle state machine (choose, resolve, animate, check end) from the rendering.
Model effects as data (id, duration, tick, stat modifiers) stored on the actor and processed each turn or second. Define stacking rules (refresh, stack or ignore) and cleanse rules up front.

A run is short, has permadeath or heavy loss, uses generated levels and offers build-defining choices (items, upgrades) that synergize. Add light meta progression between runs so failure still yields something.
Make items modify shared stats or trigger shared tags (fire, projectile, on-hit) so they combine in unplanned ways. Limit raw stat bumps and favor items that change behavior.

Build enemy waves from scripted paths (sine, arc, spiral) and bullet patterns (aimed, fan, ring) driven by time. Keep the player hitbox smaller than the sprite, use bullets with high contrast and increase density gradually.
Reward skill with multipliers that grow from chained actions and reset on mistakes, store a persistent high score, and show score changes on screen. Risk-based bonuses invite mastery and replay.

Store the snake as an ordered array of grid cells, step on a fixed tick, add a new head in the movement direction and drop the tail unless food was eaten. Queue at most one turn per tick and reject reversal into the neck; end the game on wall or body collision and spawn food only on free cells.
Build puzzles from a few rules with deep interactions, introduce rules one at a time and check every level with a solver. Provide undo and restart; the player should feel clever, not tricked.

After a swap, scan rows and columns for runs of three or more, remove them, apply gravity per column, refill from above and repeat until no matches remain (cascades). Reject swaps that create no match and generate boards without initial matches.

Define enemy paths (or flow fields), tower stats (range, damage, rate, cost) and waves as data. Balance with wave difficulty budgets, offer tower roles (single target, splash, slow) and let the player sell towers for partial refunds.

Meaningful strategy needs scarce resources, information the player must scout for and counters between unit types (rock-paper-scissors). Give the player clear selection, command and feedback UI and keep the AI opponent's rules simple but pressuring.
For hex grids use axial coordinates (q, r) with cube distance max(|dq|, |dr|, |dq+dr|), and convert to pixels with the standard pointy or flat layout formulas. Neighbors are six fixed offsets.

Top-down cars feel good with a forward speed, a steering rate that scales with speed, lateral friction that kills sideways velocity (less for drifting) and gentle off-road drag. Add camera lag and tire marks for sense of speed.

Integrate with semi-implicit Euler (update velocity then position), apply gravity as acceleration, resolve collisions with restitution and friction coefficients and keep a fixed step for stability. Use damping to stop endless jitter.

Costs grow exponentially (cost = base * 1.15^owned) while production grows linearly or by multipliers. Add offline progress by computing elapsed time on load, frequent small milestones, and prestige resets that grant permanent bonuses.

Model draw pile, hand, discard pile and exhaust pile; shuffle the discard back when the draw pile empties. Cards are data (cost, effect list) executed by a shared effect resolver so new cards need no new code.

Represent story as a graph of nodes (text, speaker, choices, conditions, effects) with flags and variables, support save and load of the current node plus flags and add a text history and skip option.

Run the world on a tick with a few interacting resources and needs, expose cause and effect through graphs and notifications, add events to disrupt steady state and avoid hidden formulas that make results feel random.

Make detection gradual (an awareness meter that fills with exposure) rather than instant, show vision cones, give guards patrol routes with pauses and offer tools to distract or hide so players can plan.
When networking is not available, deliver multiplayer as local hot-seat or same-keyboard play, or as asynchronous play against recorded ghosts and AI opponents with distinct personalities.
Support portrait and landscape by laying out UI relative to the canvas size, avoid hover-only interactions and keep important controls within thumb reach.
Target 16.6 ms per frame. Profile before optimizing, cull off-screen objects, limit particles, avoid per-frame allocation and prefer typed arrays and simple loops in hot paths.

Add a debug overlay (fps, entity counts, hitboxes) toggled by a key, make the simulation deterministic with a seed and expose a headless step function so automated tests can play many frames and assert invariants.

Script bots that press random or goal-directed inputs for thousands of frames and check invariants: no exceptions, score or state changes, player stays in bounds, game can be won and lost, restart works. This catches softlocks without a human.

A shippable small game has a title screen, instructions, a win and lose condition, increasing challenge, feedback for every action, pause, restart, sound with a mute option and no console errors. Check each item before declaring done.

Cut features before cutting quality: finish a complete vertical slice (one polished level with all systems) before adding breadth. Rank features by player impact versus effort and drop the low-impact ones first.

In Godot build reusable scenes (Player, Enemy, Bullet) with a root node and child nodes, instance them in parent scenes and communicate upward with signals and downward with direct calls. Keep scenes self-contained.

GDScript uses indentation, typed variables (var speed: float = 200.0), @export for editor properties, @onready for node references, func _ready, _process(delta) and _physics_process(delta). Use signal declarations and emit with signal_name.emit(args).

Use CharacterBody2D, set velocity each physics frame and call move_and_slide(). Read Input.get_vector for top-down movement and use is_on_floor() with gravity for platformers; multiply gravity by delta.

Define actions in the Input Map and read them with Input.is_action_pressed or Input.is_action_just_pressed. Actions can be created at runtime with InputMap.add_action and InputEventKey for generated projects.
Connect signals with signal.connect(callable). Use groups (add_to_group, get_tree().get_nodes_in_group) to find all enemies or pickups without hard references.

Set collision_layer to what an object is and collision_mask to what it detects. Use Area2D for pickups and hitboxes (body_entered signal) and CharacterBody2D for solid actors; keep layers named in project settings.

Godot 4 uses TileMapLayer nodes with a TileSet that defines physics, navigation and custom data per tile. Paint tiles with set_cell(coords, source_id, atlas_coords) and read tile data from get_cell_tile_data.

Build UI with Control nodes inside a CanvasLayer so it ignores camera movement. Use containers (VBoxContainer, HBoxContainer, MarginContainer) for layout, Label and ProgressBar for HUD and theme resources for consistent style.

Create a tween with create_tween() and chain tween_property(node, property, final, duration) for flashes, movement and UI transitions. Use AnimationPlayer or AnimatedSprite2D for frame animation and Timer nodes for delays.

Add a Camera2D as a child of the player or follow it in code, enable position smoothing, set limits to the map and implement shake by offsetting the camera's offset property with decaying random values.

Without imported art, draw shapes in _draw() using draw_rect, draw_circle, draw_polygon and draw_line, and call queue_redraw() when visuals change. Generate textures at runtime with Image and ImageTexture when needed.
Play sounds through AudioStreamPlayer nodes; generate simple tones at runtime with AudioStreamGenerator if there are no audio files, and control levels through audio buses.
Use NavigationAgent2D with a NavigationRegion2D, set target_position, then each physics frame move toward get_next_path_position(). Alternatively build an AStarGrid2D for tile-based pathfinding.

Common Godot 4 errors come from Godot 3 names: use CharacterBody2D not KinematicBody2D, @export not export, @onready not onready, move_and_slide() without arguments, signal.connect not connect(string), and randf_range or randi_range for random numbers.
Organize a browser game into modules for input, state, update, render and audio with one requestAnimationFrame loop. Keep game state in plain objects separate from DOM and rendering for testability.

Common bugs: using Array.splice while iterating forward, forgetting to reset state on restart, comparing floats exactly, modifying a collection during iteration, storing references to destroyed entities and letting timers keep running after game over. Iterate backward or filter into a new array.

For each core action ask: is there anticipation, instant response, visual impact, sound, camera or time effect and a clear result? Polishing these on the main verb has more effect than adding features.

Start from the player's stated idea and genre, then add one distinctive twist in mechanics (not just colors): a new verb, a constraint, an interaction between systems. Avoid reusing the same template for different briefs.

Re-read the user's brief before each phase and list every explicit requirement (genre, characters, rules, controls). Check the finished game against that list; the explicit requirements outrank the team's preferences.
Vary encounters, pacing and visuals every few minutes with new enemies, mechanics or environments. Escalate toward a climax and then give a resolution or a reward.
Every key action needs a distinct sound; pitch up for rewards, down for damage, short and punchy for frequent sounds and layered for big moments. Add simple music loops that change with intensity.
Spawn short-lived particles with random velocity, gravity, shrinking size and fading alpha for hits, pickups and footsteps. Use a pool and limit counts so effects do not affect frame rate.
Use easing (ease-out for arrivals, ease-in-out for moves, overshoot or elastic for pops) instead of linear interpolation for UI and effects. Cubic ease-out is t' = 1 - (1 - t)^3.

A one-page design lists the player fantasy, core loop, controls, win and lose conditions, main systems, content list and a first playable milestone. Short, specific designs produce better code than long vague ones.

Keep a small engine layer (loop, input, audio, assets, collision helpers, camera, UI helpers) independent of any one game so each new game spends effort on its own rules and content instead of rebuilding plumbing.
